content: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) is a global initiative aimed at uniting professional organizations to reduce the mortality associated with sepsis. The primary goal of the SSC is to establish an international collaborative effort to enhance the treatment of sepsis and decrease the high mortality rates linked to this condition. This is achieved through a six-pronged approach: 1. Raising awareness about sepsis. 2. Improving the accuracy and timeliness of sepsis diagnosis. 3. Promoting the use of appropriate and evidence-based treatments. 4. Educating healthcare professionals on best practices for sepsis management. 5. Enhancing post-ICU care for sepsis survivors. 6. Developing and implementing standardized care guidelines while facilitating data collection for audit and feedback purposes. The SSC, in collaboration with the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, set a goal to achieve a 25% reduction in sepsis-related mortality by 2009. Severe sepsis continues to have a high mortality rate, ranging from 30% to 50%. When septic shock is present, mortality rates increase further, reaching approximately 50% to 60%. Globally, around 1,400 people die from sepsis every day. In the United States alone, there are approximately 750,000 new cases of sepsis annually, with at least 210,000 fatalities. Similar statistics are reported across Europe. As medical advancements lead to more invasive procedures and increased use of immunosuppressive therapies, the incidence of sepsis is expected to rise further. The use of care bundles in healthcare simplifies the complex processes involved in managing patients with severe sepsis. A care bundle is a carefully selected set of evidence-based interventions that, when implemented together, have a greater impact on patient outcomes than when implemented individually. While each hospital's sepsis protocol may be customized, it must adhere to the standards established by the care bundle. The SSC Resuscitation Bundle for the first six hours of care includes the following key elements: Obtaining blood cultures before administering antibiotics. Measuring serum lactate levels. Administering broad-spectrum antibiotics within two hours of admission or diagnosis. Further management of sepsis focuses on Early Goal-Directed Therapy (EGDT). This includes maintaining blood glucose levels below 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) using an insulin sliding scale regimen, typically with short-acting insulin such as Human Actrapid. For mechanically ventilated patients, a lung-protective ventilator strategy is employed, utilizing tidal volumes of 5–8 mL/kg to minimize the risks of volutrauma and barotrauma.
